newsitem.title: GERMANY: East Germany's Wochenpost to cease publication.
newsitem.headline: East Germany's Wochenpost to cease publication.

text.p: The former East Germany's popular weekly Wochenpost, which tried unsuccessfully to woo affluent westerners after German unity, admitted defeat on Thursday and said it would cease publication at the end of the year.

The paper will not disappear entirely, but will go the way of much of east Germany's industry following unification in 1990 and be absorbed into a western weekly, Die Woche, as a supplement focusing on life in the east.

Dietrich von Boetticher, the publisher who took over Wochenpost a year ago from Gruner+Jahr, Germany's biggest magazine publisher, said in a statement that at last count the paper's distribution had fallen to a meagre 105,000 copies.
Manfred Bissinger, publisher of Die Woche, said he felt committed to publication of the Wochenpost and its future would be more secure by folding it into the western paper.

"Readers of Die Woche in west Germany will become more familiar with developments in east Germany and previous Wochenpost subscribers will benefit from the broad spectrum of issues in Die Woche," he said.

During the grey days of communist rule in East Germany, the Wochenpost flourished as one of the few bright spots, giving educated eastern Germans an alternative lifestyle and culture broadsheet in sharp contrast to party-dominated newspapers.

But after the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, it was sold to western publishers who tried to take the newspaper beyond east Germany but met a western audience largely indifferent to daily concerns of their eastern brethren.
As a result, the paper's western publishers broadened the coverage to appeal to the west and thereby began to alienate their original readers until support for paper faded.
